facts.fact: Max Poll described the species in 1939.
ITIS lists Steatocranus casuarius Poll, 1939 as a valid name.
The genus name combines Greek steatos (hard fat) and kranion (skull).
Steatocranus elongatus is given as a synonym.
The Glaser page counts eight species in the genus, some of them quite similar.
It is often confused with S. gibbiceps, which comes from the same Congo region and is exported with it.
Scale centres separate the two: dark in S. casuarius, light in S. gibbiceps.
The slender buffalo head (S. tinanti) is more streamlined than this species and has a very large mouth.
The swim bladder is reduced, so the fish is less buoyant and can hold position in strong flow.
The modified swim bladder keeps it from being swept away.
It moves over the bottom in short hops.
The nuchal hump can change size quite quickly.
Body shape is elongated.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern, assessed 16 February 2009.
It lives in Pool Malebo (Stanley Pool) and the lower Congo River.
Its range covers both the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
It comes from the lower Congo basin.
It occurs in the Lower Congo River and its tributaries.
It lives in very fast rapids.
It inhabits fast, turbulent stretches of river, usually in pockets of still water.
In the wild it colonises boulder bottoms in rapids.
It is a rheophilic, bottom-dwelling freshwater fish.
It is found in rocky rapids of the lower Zaire (Congo) River.
It is commercially traded for aquaria.
Wild-caught and captive-bred fish have both been stocked by the German wholesaler Aquarium Glaser, at 4-6 cm and 3-4 cm.
Buying an established pair or juveniles is advised, because unpaired fish often do poorly.
Hobby sources often call it hyper-aggressive; the video's keepers disagree after years of keeping it.
A 40-gallon tank is the smallest suggested for a pair.
Two pairs may fit in 40 gallons with plenty of rock and broken sight lines.
A group of six or more needs at least 75 gallons.
A tank of 75 × 30 × 30 cm is given as the base size.
A minimum aquarium of 80 cm, with fish kept in pairs, is recommended.
A 20-gallon tank is said to suit one pair.
Another guide asks for at least 50 gallons.
Rock piles, stacked hardscape and soft sand suit it, since it digs and burrows.
Rock caves should be fixed to the tank base or siliconed so digging cannot bring them down.
Use robust, potted or weighted plants, because the fish burrows.
Temperature of 75-82°F and pH 6-8 are suggested, with stable water more important than exact values.
It enjoys fast flow and needs well-oxygenated water.
Seriously Fish gives 24-28°C, pH 6.0-7.5 and 2-15 dGH.
A powerhead for strong flow is advised, along with a low-flow area.
FishBase gives 24-28°C, pH 6.0-8.0 and dH 5-19.
It needs soft water that is not excessively acidic.
One guide gives an alkaline pH of 7.5-8.5, unlike the other sources.
One profile allows a temperature of 24-30°C.
In aquaria it takes flake, pellet, frozen and live food.
Food must sink to the bottom or the rock pile, because it will not rise to feed.
In the wild it is reported to feed primarily on algae.
It accepts dried food, but live and frozen foods such as bloodworm and brine shrimp should be added.
Food should not be too fatty; Tubifex and similar foods can cause fatal intestinal disease.
It is an omnivore needing both meaty food and plant matter.
Chopped freshwater mussel is often relished and can help tempt difficult feeders.
The video's keepers call it territorial rather than aggressive.
It stays low and does not swim above mid-level, but climbs and sits on stacked rocks.
It ignores tetras, barbs and other fish using the mid to upper water.
It chases and bumps other cichlids that enter its territory, especially when spawning.
The video's keepers keep the genus with small cichlids of 3-4 inches without torn fins or hiding.
It pushes with its head; biting or fin nipping was not seen by the video's keepers.
Pairs are best, and other cichlids should be avoided unless the tank is very large.
Suggested tankmates include alestiid tetras, larger characins, barbs and rheophilic Synodontis.
It is relatively peaceful, but strongly defends the area around its breeding cave.
Plants are occasionally dug up or bitten when the fish are breeding.
It is described as territorial and pugnacious, more so during spawning, though it can live with many larger fish.
A fish that loses its mate usually lives alone afterwards.
Mature males can be aggressive towards females, and new mates often fail to bond.
Males are larger and develop a bigger nuchal hump than females.
Males reach about 12 cm and females about 8 cm.
Males reach about 6 inches and females about 4 inches, by this profile.
Males have longer fins than females.
Males grow longer and are darker than females.
In aquaria it is pretty easy to breed and will likely spawn if its needs are met.
It is a pair-bonding cave spawner producing 20-150 eggs.
In aquaria, a species tank with Congo tetras as dither fish, at 24-26.5°C and pH 6.0-7.0, is suggested.
Eggs hatch in about 5-7 days and fry swim freely after 11-14 days, in aquaria.
Both parents guard the brood for up to 3 months in aquaria.
A pair digs a cave under a rock and the female lays eggs on its roof and sides, in aquaria.
One profile reports hatching in about 3-4 days and free-swimming fry around day 5, in aquaria.
Clutches in aquaria are typically 30-60 eggs, with up to 150 possible.
For aquarium breeding this source gives pH 6.5-6.9, 4-12 dH and 27-29°C, with caves or overturned flowerpots.
In aquaria the female guards the eggs while the male guards the territory.
Fry can be fed Artemia nauplii and dry foods.
Pairs bond for life and may spawn on a cave roof or inside a shell, in aquaria.
